article.title: Japan to revise national security policy, weaken postwar non-nuclear commitments
article.author: Abdul Rahman
article.content: Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) claimed on Monday, November 23, that it will revise the country’s three security documents by the end of the year and possibly acquire nuclear-power submarines soon. Civil society groups on China and Japan have been opposing the decision, calling it a move towards remilitarization. They also claim such a move would be disastrous for regional peace and security and for the post-war regional order. Keitaro Ohno, a leader of the LDP and a member of Japanese parliament reportedly reiterated that Japan has rejected the proposal to get a nuclear-powered submarine in the wake of strong popular opposition and objections raised by China. He also claimed there is a consensus within the ruling coalition on the matter. The conservative LDP, along with the right wing Japan Innovation Party (JIP), holds a supermajority in the House of Representative (lower house) of Japan’s National Diet (parliament). On Friday, Japan’s civil society groups had submitted 47,000 signatures to the country’s Defense Ministry, urging it to abandon the plan to acquire nuclear-powered submarines and amendments in the security documents. Japan has also recorded several popular mobilizations against the Sanae Takaichi-led government’s moves to revise the three security documents, including its three non-nuclear principles, which prohibit its government from acquiring, producing, or introducing nuclear weapons. Still, reports indicate that the Japanese government is aiming to make changes in its National Security Strategy, one of the three security documents, within the next few months, to allow nuclear weapons to be brought in the country during an “emergency.” Civil society groups expressed concerns at the Takaichi government’s attempts to introduce nuclear weapons in the country even under this pretense, claiming it violates one of the three non-nuclear principles of not introducing the weapons. They claimed once Japan moves ahead with the acquisition it will fundamentally alter the country’s status from a non-nuclear weapons’ state to a nuclear weapons state and this will go against its stated responsibility to promote nuclear disarmament. Japan’s commitment to nuclear disarmament is rooted in the fact that it remains the only country in the world which has faced nuclear attacks. Impact on relations with China China has warned successive Japanese governments including Takaichi against any attempt to re-militarize the country claiming any such move would shake the balance in the region and will lead to instability and arms race. Read more: China urges Japan to abandon nuclear ambitions and respect international law China has demanded that the international community check the Japanese government to keep it from violating its commitments to the post-war order, drawing their attention to Japan’s imperial past and its devastating impact on all other nations in the region, including China. Though several Japanese governments in the last few years have expressed “revivalist” intentions and talked about re-militarization of the country, the Takaichi government has made significant efforts in that direction despite Chinese objections and risks of confrontation. Earlier this year, Takaichi even talked about military intervention in case China attempts to integrate Taiwan militarily. She made the comments despite a long standing Japanese commitment to “One-China” policy. China reacted strongly to her statement and demanded she apologize. However, Takaichi refused to apologize or withdraw her statement, which created prolonged diplomatic tension between the two countries. During last week’s visit to Shenzen, China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Summit (APEC) she, however, reaffirmed her government’s commitments to the 1972 Japan-China Joint Statement and four political documents signed by the two countries, indicating moderation. Reacting to her statement, Guo Jiakun, spokesperson of China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said last week that Japan must fulfill its political responsibility and legal obligations towards China as described in the four documents – not just verbally but through “concrete action.” “For Japan, the pressing priority is to correct the erroneous words and moves on the Taiwan question, adopt a correct attitude on historical issues, and form an objective and rational perception on China,” Guo said.
